source: High-throughput transgenesis using synthetic DNA libraries is a powerful method for systematically exploring genetic function.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of high-throughput transgenesis, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

source: Diverse synthesized libraries have been used for protein engineering, identification of protein–protein interactions, characterization of promoter libraries, developmental and evolutionary lineage tracking, and various other exploratory assays.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and practice in the field, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

source: However, the need for library transgenesis has effectively restricted these approaches to single-cell models.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current transgenesis methods in multicellular organisms, as discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: TARDIS is a simple yet powerful approach to large-scale transgenesis that overcomes typical limitations encountered in multicellular systems.
source: Here, we present Transgenic Arrays Resulting in Diversity of Integrated Sequences (TARDIS), a simple yet powerful approach to large-scale transgenesis that overcomes typical limitations encountered in multicellular systems.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: TARDIS splits the transgenesis process into a two-step process: creation of individuals carrying experimentally introduced sequence libraries, followed by inducible extraction and integration of individual sequences/library components from the larger library cassette into engineered genomic sites.
source: TARDIS splits the transgenesis process into a two-step process: creation of individuals carrying experimentally introduced sequence libraries, followed by inducible extraction and integration of individual sequences/library components from the larger library cassette into engineered genomic sites.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of TARDIS, which is demonstrated experimentally in the manuscript.

claim: Transformation of a single individual, followed by lineage expansion and functional transgenesis, gives rise to thousands of genetically unique transgenic individuals.
source: Thus, transformation of a single individual, followed by lineage expansion and functional transgenesis, gives rise to thousands of genetically unique transgenic individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results showing recovery of thousands of unique barcodes and multiple promoter integrations.

claim: TARDIS was used to generate a large set of individually barcoded lineages in C. elegans.
source: We demonstrate the power of this system using engineered, split selectable TARDIS sites in Caenorhabditis elegans to generate (1) a large set of individually barcoded lineages and (2) transcriptional reporter lines from predefined promoter libraries.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the barcode experiments described in the Results section.

claim: TARDIS was used to generate transcriptional reporter lines from predefined promoter libraries in C. elegans.
source: We demonstrate the power of this system using engineered, split selectable TARDIS sites in Caenorhabditis elegans to generate (1) a large set of individually barcoded lineages and (2) transcriptional reporter lines from predefined promoter libraries.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the promoter library experiments described in the Results section.

claim: TARDIS increases transformation yields up to approximately 1000-fold over current single-step methods.
source: We find that this approach increases transformation yields up to approximately 1000-fold over current single-step methods.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of the number of unique integrations obtained with TARDIS versus traditional methods.

claim: The TARDIS process is adaptable to any system where experimentally generated genomic loci landing pads and diverse, heritable DNA elements can be generated.
source: While we demonstrate the utility of TARDIS using C. elegans, in principle the process is adaptable to any system where experimentally generated genomic loci landing pads and diverse, heritable DNA elements can be generated.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential applicability of TARDIS to other systems, based on the conceptual design of the method.

claim: Transgenesis has been a central tool for functional analysis and genetic engineering for nearly 40 years.
source: Transgenesis, which is the specific and heritable introduction of foreign DNA into genomes, has been a central tool for functional analysis and genetic engineering for nearly 40 y.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge and the history of molecular biology.

claim: Most uses of transgenesis can be grouped into those inserting a small number of known sequences (specific transgenesis) and those introducing many sequence variants from experimental libraries (exploratory transgenesis).
source: While there are many uses for transgenesis, in practice most can be grouped into those inserting a small number of known sequences (specific transgenesis) and those introducing many sequence variants from experimental libraries (exploratory transgenesis).
evidence: This is a conceptual categorization based on common practices in the field.

claim: Exploratory transgenesis remains effectively limited to single-cell models because of biological limitations generated by inheritance in multicellular organisms.
source: While the ability to perform specific transgenesis has become a de facto requirement for all model organisms, exploratory transgenesis remains effectively limited to single-cell models (both prokaryotic and eukaryotic) because of biological limitations generated by inheritance in multicellular organisms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical challenges of transgenesis in multicellular organisms, particularly the Weismann barrier.

claim: High-throughput transgenesis in single-cell models has been used for exploratory sampling of sequence space using protein interaction libraries.
source: In single-cell models, high-throughput transgenesis has been used for exploratory sampling of sequence space using protein interaction libraries (Joung et al., 2000), barcode-lineage tracking libraries (Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019), directed evolution (Packer and Liu, 2015), synthetic promoter library screens (Wu et al., 2019), and mutagenesis screens (Bock et al., 2022; Erwood et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022; Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Joung et al., 2000.

claim: High-throughput transgenesis in single-cell models has been used for barcode-lineage tracking libraries.
source: In single-cell models, high-throughput transgenesis has been used for exploratory sampling of sequence space using protein interaction libraries (Joung et al., 2000), barcode-lineage tracking libraries (Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019), directed evolution (Packer and Liu, 2015), synthetic promoter library screens (Wu et al., 2019), and mutagenesis screens (Bock et al., 2022; Erwood et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022; Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Levy et al., 2015 and Nguyen Ba et al., 2019.

claim: High-throughput transgenesis in single-cell models has been used for directed evolution.
source: In single-cell models, high-throughput transgenesis has been used for exploratory sampling of sequence space using protein interaction libraries (Joung et al., 2000), barcode-lineage tracking libraries (Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019), directed evolution (Packer and Liu, 2015), synthetic promoter library screens (Wu et al., 2019), and mutagenesis screens (Bock et al., 2022; Erwood et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022; Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Packer and Liu, 2015.

claim: High-throughput transgenesis in single-cell models has been used for synthetic promoter library screens.
source: In single-cell models, high-throughput transgenesis has been used for exploratory sampling of sequence space using protein interaction libraries (Joung et al., 2000), barcode-lineage tracking libraries (Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019), directed evolution (Packer and Liu, 2015), synthetic promoter library screens (Wu et al., 2019), and mutagenesis screens (Bock et al., 2022; Erwood et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022; Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Wu et al., 2019.

claim: High-throughput transgenesis in single-cell models has been used for mutagenesis screens.
source: In single-cell models, high-throughput transgenesis has been used for exploratory sampling of sequence space using protein interaction libraries (Joung et al., 2000), barcode-lineage tracking libraries (Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019), directed evolution (Packer and Liu, 2015), synthetic promoter library screens (Wu et al., 2019), and mutagenesis screens (Bock et al., 2022; Erwood et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022; Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Bock et al., 2022; Erwood et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2022; Sánchez-Rivera et al., 2022.

claim: Increasing transgenic throughput in multicellular models holds the potential to expand the impact of exploratory transgenesis in functional domains such as inter-tissue signaling, neuronal health, and animal behavior.
source: Despite the usefulness of such experiments in single-celled systems, either in microorganisms or in cell culture, increasing transgenic throughput in multicellular models holds the potential to expand the impact of exploratory transgenesis in functional domains, such as inter-tissue signaling, neuronal health, and animal behavior, that are dependent on multicellular interactions and therefore difficult to replicate in single-cell models.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential applications of high-throughput transgenesis in multicellular systems.

claim: Exploratory transgenesis in single-cell models has been facilitated by the availability of in vitro-generated DNA libraries, selectable markers, plasmids, in vivo homologous recombination, and the ability to massively parallelize transgenesis.
source: Exploratory transgenesis in single-cell models has been facilitated by the availability of in vitro-generated DNA libraries, selectable markers, plasmids, in vivo homologous recombination, and most importantly, the ability to massively parallelize transgenesis using microbial transformation or eukaryotic cell transfection/transduction.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of techniques used in single-cell systems.

claim: There is no practical means to make populations of uniquely transgenic individuals from sequence libraries at a similar scale in animal systems due to the Weismann barrier.
source: Currently, there is no practical means to make populations of uniquely transgenic individuals from sequence libraries at a similar scale in animal systems due to the Weismann barrier (Weismann, 1893): the split between soma and germline.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Weismann, 1893, and reflects the technical challenges in animal transgenesis.

claim: The requirement that the germline be accessible and editable has forced animal systems into a transgenic bottleneck compared to single-cell systems.
source: The requirement that the germline be accessible and editable has forced animal systems into a transgenic bottleneck compared to single-cell systems because it is very difficult to introduce exogenous DNA directly into the germline in a high-throughput manner, relying instead on injection, bombardment, or some other physical intervention.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical limitations of germline manipulation in animals.

claim: The low-throughput limitation in animals dramatically reduces the sequence diversity that can be sampled, effectively preventing large-scale exploratory experiments from being performed.
source: This low-throughput limitation in animals dramatically reduces the sequence diversity that can be sampled, effectively preventing large-scale exploratory experiments from being performed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical constraints of animal transgenesis.

claim: Brainbow is an attempt to parallelize transgenic creation in multicellular model organisms.
source: Attempts have been made to parallelize transgenic creation in multicellular model organisms, for example, the development of Brainbow (Livet et al., 2007; Weissman and Pan, 2015), ifgMosaic analysis (Pontes-Quero et al., 2017), P[acman] libraries in Drosophila (Venken et al., 2009), and multiple types of transformation in plants (Ismagul et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Livet et al., 2007 and Weissman and Pan, 2015.

claim: ifgMosaic analysis is an attempt to parallelize transgenic creation in multicellular model organisms.
source: Attempts have been made to parallelize transgenic creation in multicellular model organisms, for example, the development of Brainbow (Livet et al., 2007; Weissman and Pan, 2015), ifgMosaic analysis (Pontes-Quero et al., 2017), P[acman] libraries in Drosophila (Venken et al., 2009), and multiple types of transformation in plants (Ismagul et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Pontes-Quero et al., 2017.

claim: P[acman] libraries in Drosophila are an attempt to parallelize transgenic creation in multicellular model organisms.
source: Attempts have been made to parallelize transgenic creation in multicellular model organisms, for example, the development of Brainbow (Livet et al., 2007; Weissman and Pan, 2015), ifgMosaic analysis (Pontes-Quero et al., 2017), P[acman] libraries in Drosophila (Venken et al., 2009), and multiple types of transformation in plants (Ismagul et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Venken et al., 2009.

claim: Multiple types of transformation in plants are attempts to parallelize transgenic creation in multicellular model organisms.
source: Attempts have been made to parallelize transgenic creation in multicellular model organisms, for example, the development of Brainbow (Livet et al., 2007; Weissman and Pan, 2015), ifgMosaic analysis (Pontes-Quero et al., 2017), P[acman] libraries in Drosophila (Venken et al., 2009), and multiple types of transformation in plants (Ismagul et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Ismagul et al., 2018 and Xu et al., 2022.

claim: CRISPR technology combined with custom engineered sites within the genome ('landing pads') has facilitated the generation of single-copy integrations in C. elegans.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, CRISPR technology combined with custom engineered sites within the genome ('landing pads') has facilitated the generation of single-copy integrations (Malaiwong et al., 2023; Nonet, 2020; Nonet, 2021; Silva-García et al., 2019; Stevenson et al., 2020; Vicencio et al., 2019), and attempts have been made to multiplex transgenesis using traditional integration methods in conjunction with specialized landing pad systems (Gilleland et al., 2015 ; Kaymak et al., 2016; Mouridi et al., 2022; Radman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Malaiwong et al., 2023; Nonet, 2020; Nonet, 2021; Silva-García et al., 2019; Stevenson et al., 2020; Vicencio et al., 2019.

claim: Attempts have been made to multiplex transgenesis in C. elegans using traditional integration methods in conjunction with specialized landing pad systems.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, CRISPR technology combined with custom engineered sites within the genome ('landing pads') has facilitated the generation of single-copy integrations (Malaiwong et al., 2023; Nonet, 2020; Nonet, 2021; Silva-García et al., 2019; Stevenson et al., 2020; Vicencio et al., 2019), and attempts have been made to multiplex transgenesis using traditional integration methods in conjunction with specialized landing pad systems (Gilleland et al., 2015 ; Kaymak et al., 2016; Mouridi et al., 2022; Radman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Gilleland et al., 2015; Kaymak et al., 2016; Mouridi et al., 2022; Radman et al., 2013.

claim: Previous efforts to increase throughput in C. elegans have increased throughput over standard single-copy integration methods, but throughput still remains too low for effective exploratory transgenesis.
source: While these efforts have increased throughput over standard single-copy integration methods, throughput still remains too low for effective exploratory transgenesis, and in some cases requires significant additional labor, cost, equipment, and/or expertise.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of existing methods with the requirements for exploratory transgenesis.

claim: TARDIS greatly expands throughput by explicitly separating and reordering the conceptual steps of transgenesis.
source: Here, we present 'Transgenic Arrays Resulting in Diversity of Integrated Sequences' (TARDIS) (Stevenson et al., 2021), a simple yet powerful alternative to traditional single-copy transgenesis. TARDIS greatly expands throughput by explicitly separating and reordering of the conceptual steps of transgenesis (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: TARDIS begins with an in vitro-generated DNA sequence library that is introduced into germ cells via traditional low-throughput methods.
source: To increase throughput, TARDIS begins with an in vitro-generated DNA sequence library that is introduced into germ cells via traditional low-throughput methods (i.e., germline transformation, Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the first step of the TARDIS method, as shown in Figure 1.

claim: In TARDIS, DNA sequences are designed to be incorporated in large numbers into diverse, heritable sub-libraries (TARDIS libraries), rather than be directly integrated into the desired genomic locus.
source: While traditional transgenesis typically couples the physical introduction of DNA into cells with the integration of a selected sequence from the original library, the DNA sequences in TARDIS are designed to be incorporated in large numbers into diverse, heritable sub-libraries (TARDIS libraries), rather than be directly integrated into the desired genomic locus.
evidence: This describes a key conceptual difference between TARDIS and traditional transgenesis.

claim: A functioning selectable marker is included in TARDIS to stabilize the inheritance of the TARDIS library over generations.
source: In addition to the sequence library, a functioning selectable marker is also included to stabilize the inheritance of the TARDIS library over generations.
evidence: This describes a component of the TARDIS method.

claim: TARDIS libraries function to create 'metaploidy' – expanding the total number of alleles available for inheritance.
source: These TARDIS libraries function to create 'metaploidy' – expanding the total number of alleles available for inheritance, essentially making the worm genetically 'bigger on the inside.'
evidence: This is a conceptual description of how TARDIS libraries function.

claim: TARDIS library-bearing animals are allowed to propagate under selection to generate a large population of TARDIS library carriers.
source: TARDIS library-bearing animals are then allowed to propagate under selection to generate a large population of TARDIS library carriers.
evidence: This describes a step in the TARDIS protocol.

claim: After population expansion, genome integration of a single-sequence unit is performed by inducing a double-strand break at a genetically engineered landing pad.
source: After population expansion, genome integration of a single-sequence unit is performed by inducing a double-strand break at a genetically engineered landing pad.
evidence: This describes the integration step of the TARDIS method.

claim: The TARDIS landing pad is designed to both integrate a sequence unit and act as a second selectable marker.
source: This landing pad is designed to both integrate a sequence unit and act as a second selectable marker.
evidence: This describes the design of the landing pad used in TARDIS.

claim: C. elegans was chosen to validate the TARDIS approach because C. elegans naturally form extrachromosomal arrays that can be several megabases in size from injected DNA.
source: We chose C. elegans to validate the TARDIS approach because C. elegans naturally form extrachromosomal arrays that can be several megabases in size (Carlton et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021; Mello et al., 1991; Stinchcomb et al., 1985) from injected DNA, which simplifies the generation of heritable 'TARDIS library arrays' (TLA) that encompass significant sequence diversity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Carlton et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021; Mello et al., 1991; Stinchcomb et al., 1985.

claim: C. elegans naturally form extrachromosomal arrays that can be several megabases in size from injected DNA.
source: We chose C. elegans to validate the TARDIS approach because C. elegans naturally form extrachromosomal arrays that can be several megabases in size (Carlton et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021; Mello et al., 1991; Stinchcomb et al., 1985) from injected DNA, which simplifies the generation of heritable 'TARDIS library arrays' (TLA) that encompass significant sequence diversity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Carlton et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2021; Mello et al., 1991; Stinchcomb et al., 1985.

claim: Barcoding has been widely adopted in microbial systems for evolutionary lineage tracking.
source: Barcoding has been widely adopted in microbial systems for evolutionary lineage tracking (Jahn et al., 2018; Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019) and for developmental lineage tracking in animals (Kebschull and Zador, 2018; McKenna et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Jahn et al., 2018; Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019.

claim: Barcoding has been widely adopted for developmental lineage tracking in animals.
source: Barcoding has been widely adopted in microbial systems for evolutionary lineage tracking (Jahn et al., 2018; Levy et al., 2015; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019) and for developmental lineage tracking in animals (Kebschull and Zador, 2018; McKenna et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Kebschull and Zador, 2018; McKenna et al., 2016.

claim: In microbial systems, barcode libraries have relied on highly diverse randomized oligo libraries.
source: In microbial systems, barcode libraries have relied on highly diverse randomized oligo libraries, compared to animal systems, which have relied on CRE recombinases or randomized Cas9-induced mutations.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of barcoding methods in different systems.

claim: In animal systems, barcode libraries have relied on CRE recombinases or randomized Cas9-induced mutations.
source: In microbial systems, barcode libraries have relied on highly diverse randomized oligo libraries, compared to animal systems, which have relied on CRE recombinases or randomized Cas9-induced mutations.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of barcoding methods in different systems.

claim: Large, heritable libraries containing thousands of barcodes can be created and maintained as extrachromosomal arrays in C. elegans.
source: Our results show that large, heritable libraries containing thousands of barcodes can be created and maintained as extrachromosomal arrays.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing recovery of thousands of unique barcodes from TARDIS arrays.

claim: Individual sequences are selected and removed from the TARDIS library upon experimental induction of Cas9 in a proportion consistent with the composition of the TLA with rare overrepresented sequences.
source: Individual sequences are selected and removed from the library upon experimental induction of Cas9 in a proportion consistent with the composition of the TLA with rare overrepresented sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data in Figure 4 showing the correlation between array frequency and integration frequency.

claim: TARDIS is compatible with the integration of large promoters.
source: We found that TARDIS is also compatible with the integration of large promoters and can be used to simultaneously integrate promoters into multiple genomic locations, providing a tool for multiple insertions at defined locations across the genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing successful integration of promoters ranging from 330 bp to 5.5 kb.

claim: TARDIS can be used to simultaneously integrate promoters into multiple genomic locations.
source: We found that TARDIS is also compatible with the integration of large promoters and can be used to simultaneously integrate promoters into multiple genomic locations, providing a tool for multiple insertions at defined locations across the genome.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing dual integration into two landing pad sites.

claim: A specific landing pad for the introduction and selection of small barcode fragments from high-diversity, multiplexed barcode libraries was designed.
source: We designed a specific landing pad for the introduction and selection of small barcode fragments from high-diversity, multiplexed barcode libraries (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes the design of the barcode landing pad, as shown in Figure 2.

claim: The barcode landing pad was designed to be targeted by Cas9 and requires perfect integration on both the 5′ and 3′ ends of a synthetic intron for functional hygromycin B resistance.
source: This landing pad was designed to be targeted by Cas9 and requires perfect integration on both the 5′ and 3′ ends of a synthetic intron for functional hygromycin B resistance.
evidence: This describes the design features of the barcode landing pad.

claim: Current split selection landing pads only provide selection on one side of the double-strand break, which can result in a small percentage of incomplete integrations.
source: Current split selection landing pads only provide selection on one side of the double-strand break, which can result in a small percentage of incomplete integrations (Stevenson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Stevenson et al., 2020.

claim: A split-selection, hygromycin resistance (HygR) system was chosen for its simplicity and integration-specific selection.
source: A split-selection, hygromycin resistance (HygR) system was chosen for its simplicity and integration-specific selection.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the choice of selectable marker.

claim: A unique synthetic CRISPR guide RNA target sequence was created by removing coding sequence on both sides of an artificial intron, resulting in a nonfunctional HygR gene.
source: A unique synthetic CRISPR guide RNA target sequence was created by removing coding sequence on both sides of an artificial intron, resulting in a nonfunctional HygR gene.
evidence: This describes the construction of the landing pad.

claim: By removing critical coding sequence on both sides of the gene, only 'perfect' integration events will result in hygromycin resistance.
source: By removing critical coding sequence on both sides of the gene, only 'perfect' integration events will result in hygromycin resistance (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the selection mechanism of the landing pad, as illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The synthetic landing pad was integrated at Chromosome II: 8,420,157, which has previously been shown to be permissive for germline expression.
source: The synthetic landing pad was integrated at Chromosome II: 8,420,157, which has previously been shown to be permissive for germline expression (Dickinson et al., 2015; Frøkjær-Jensen et al., 2012; Frøkjaer-Jensen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations to Dickinson et al., 2015; Frøkjær-Jensen et al., 2012; Frøkjaer-Jensen et al., 2008.

claim: Oligo libraries have been used for barcoding in yeast.
source: Oligo libraries have been used for barcoding (Levy et al., 2015) and for identification of promoter elements (de Boer et al., 2020) in yeast, but practical implementation of large synthetic libraries for transgenesis has never been performed in an animal system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Levy et al., 2015.

claim: Oligo libraries have been used for identification of promoter elements in yeast.
source: Oligo libraries have been used for barcoding (Levy et al., 2015) and for identification of promoter elements (de Boer et al., 2020) in yeast, but practical implementation of large synthetic libraries for transgenesis has never been performed in an animal system.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to de Boer et al., 2020.

claim: Practical implementation of large synthetic libraries for transgenesis has never been performed in an animal system.
source: Oligo libraries have been used for barcoding (Levy et al., 2015) and for identification of promoter elements (de Boer et al., 2020) in yeast, but practical implementation of large synthetic libraries for transgenesis has never been performed in an animal system.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the TARDIS approach, based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Randomized synthesized oligos were used to build a highly diverse library of barcodes via complexing PCR.
source: We used randomized synthesized oligos to build a highly diverse library of barcodes, similar to the one described by Levy et al., 2015, via complexing PCR.
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the barcode library.

claim: The base barcode library can yield a theoretical maximum of approximately 4.2 million sequences given randomized bases present at the 11 nucleotide positions centrally located within the barcode.
source: Given randomized bases present at the 11 nucleotide positions centrally located within the barcode, our base library can yield a theoretical maximum of approximately 4.2 million sequences.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the design of the barcode library (4^11 ≈ 4.2 million).

claim: The overlap PCR approach achieves high levels of diversity with minimal 'jackpotting' – sequences with higher representation than expected.
source: Our overlap PCR approach achieves high levels of diversity with minimal 'jackpotting' – sequences with higher representation than expected (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: With low-coverage sequencing, almost 800,000 unique barcode sequences were found in the injection mix.
source: With low-coverage sequencing, we found almost 800,000 unique barcode sequences, providing a large pool of potential sequences that can be incorporated into TARDIS arrays.
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequencing data.

claim: Only 472 sequences were overrepresented (counts greater than 50) in the injection mix, accounting for approximately 6.7% of the total reads and only approximately 0.06% of the unique barcodes detected.
source: Only 472 sequences were overrepresented (counts greater than 50), accounting for approximately 6.7% of the total reads and only approximately 0.06% of the unique barcodes detected.
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequencing data analysis.

claim: Four arrays were isolated from three plates after injection of the barcode library.
source: We injected our complexed barcodes and isolated individual TARDIS array lines, each containing a subset of the barcode library (Figure 3). Individual injected worms were singled, and we identified four arrays from three plates.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment.

claim: Arrays 1 and 2 were identified on separate plates, and were therefore derived from independent array formation events.
source: Arrays 1 and 2 were identified on separate plates, and were therefore derived from independent array formation events, while array 3, profile 1 and array 3, profile 2 were both identified on the same plate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: Array 3, profile 1 and array 3, profile 2 were both identified on the same plate.
source: Arrays 1 and 2 were identified on separate plates, and were therefore derived from independent array formation events, while array 3, profile 1 and array 3, profile 2 were both identified on the same plate.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the experiment.

claim: During array formation a subset of barcode sequences tended to increase in frequency.
source: Analysis of array diversity within these lines shows, somewhat unexpectedly, that during array formation a subset of barcode sequences tended to increase in frequency (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Higher frequency barcodes in arrays tend to be independent of the jackpotted sequences of the injection mix.
source: Higher frequency barcodes in arrays tend to be independent of the jackpotted sequences of the injection mix as very few are represented in the set of high-frequency barcodes from the injection mix.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the high-frequency barcodes in arrays versus the injection mix.

claim: The high-frequency barcodes varied between arrays.
source: The high-frequency barcodes also varied between arrays.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the barcode frequencies across different arrays.

claim: Array formation does not seem to favor any particular barcode sequence motif.
source: We found that array formation does not seem to favor any particular barcode sequence motif (Figure 3C) and that arrays can range considerably in diversity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Arrays can range considerably in diversity.
source: We found that array formation does not seem to favor any particular barcode sequence motif (Figure 3C) and that arrays can range considerably in diversity.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that different arrays contained different numbers of unique barcodes.

claim: Array 1 had 1319 unique barcode sequences.
source: Array 1 had 1319 unique barcode sequences, array 2 had 3001 unique barcode sequences, array 3 profile 1 had 91 unique barcode sequences, and array 3 profile 2 had 204 unique barcode sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequencing data.

claim: Array 2 had 3001 unique barcode sequences.
source: Array 1 had 1319 unique barcode sequences, array 2 had 3001 unique barcode sequences, array 3 profile 1 had 91 unique barcode sequences, and array 3 profile 2 had 204 unique barcode sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequencing data.

claim: Array 3 profile 1 had 91 unique barcode sequences.
source: Array 1 had 1319 unique barcode sequences, array 2 had 3001 unique barcode sequences, array 3 profile 1 had 91 unique barcode sequences, and array 3 profile 2 had 204 unique barcode sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct observation from sequencing data.

claim: Array 3 profile 2 had 204 unique barcode sequences.
source: Array 1 had 1319 unique barcode sequences, array 2 had 3001 unique barcode sequences, array 3 profile 1 had 91 unique barcode sequences, and array 3 profile 2 had 204 unique barcode sequences (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
